claim: Sleep is a dynamic process in most animals, involving distinct stages that probably perform multiple functions for the brain.
source: Sleep is a dynamic process in most animals, involving distinct stages that probably perform multiple functions for the brain.
evidence: This is a general statement about sleep that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: Before sleep functions can be initiated, it is likely that behavioral responsiveness to the outside world needs to be reduced, even while the animal is still awake.
source: Before sleep functions can be initiated, it is likely that behavioral responsiveness to the outside world needs to be reduced, even while the animal is still awake.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the relationship between behavioral responsiveness and sleep initiation.

claim: Recent work in Drosophila has uncovered a sleep switch in the dorsal fan-shaped body (dFB) of the fly's central brain.
source: Recent work in Drosophila has uncovered a sleep switch in the dorsal fan-shaped body (dFB) of the fly's central brain
evidence: This statement references prior research findings about the dFB as a sleep switch.

claim: Optogenetic activation of the sleep switch suppressed behavioral responsiveness to mechanical stimuli, even in awake flies.
source: We found that optogenetic activation of the sleep switch suppressed behavioral responsiveness to mechanical stimuli, even in awake flies
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments using optogenetics.

claim: The dFB-mediated suppression mechanism and its associated neural correlates requires innexin6 expression.
source: The dFB-mediated suppression mechanism and its associated neural correlates requires innexin6 expression
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with innexin6 knockdown.

claim: The acute need to reduce sensory perception when flies fall asleep is mediated in part by electrical synapses.
source: suggesting that the acute need to reduce sensory perception when flies fall asleep is mediated in part by electrical synapses.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the innexin6 findings, as innexins form gap junctions (electrical synapses).

claim: Some proposed sleep functions may be deeply conserved across all animals.
source: Most animals sleep, and recent research suggests that some proposed sleep functions may be deeply conserved across all animals (Cirelli, 2009; Kirszenblat and van Swinderen, 2015; Zimmerman et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Sleep functions range from cellular stress regulation in nematodes to synaptic homeostasis and memory consolidation in mammals.
source: These functions range from cellular stress regulation in nematodes (Hill et al., 2014; Nelson et al., 2014) to synaptic homeostasis and memory consolidation in mammals (Rasch and Born, 2013; Tononi and Cirelli, 2006; Tononi and Cirelli, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Sleep may serve to maintain cellular health by clearing protein debris.
source: Other proposed functions of sleep include maintaining cellular health, by clearing of protein debris for example (Xie et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Conserved cellular processes might have been integrated through evolution into distinct stages of the mammalian sleep cycle.
source: These conserved cellular processes might have been integrated through evolution into distinct stages of the mammalian sleep cycle, to accommodate multiple more recent sleep functions, such as synaptic scaling and memory consolidation, simultaneously (Kirszenblat and van Swinderen, 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about evolutionary integration of sleep functions, supported by a citation.

claim: In most animals sleep results largely from widespread changes in electrical activity throughout the brain.
source: Although sleep may serve many diverse functions, and although many different molecular processes might be involved, in most animals sleep is understood to result largely from widespread changes in electrical activity throughout the brain.
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific understanding about sleep mechanisms.

claim: The rapidly reversible switch that allows sleep functions to take place probably requires important changes in electrical activity in the brain to decrease behavioral responsiveness.
source: That is, the rapidly reversible switch that allows the aforementioned potential functions to take place probably requires important changes in electrical activity in the brain: initially to decrease behavioral responsiveness and thereby allow some of these processes to proceed without ongoing behavioral interference (Mednick et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism of sleep switches, supported by a citation.

claim: In mammals, dis-inhibition of GABAergic sleep-promoting neurons in the vasolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO) is thought to comprise part of a sleep switch.
source: In mammals, dis-inhibition of GABAergic sleep-promoting neurons in the vasolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO) is thought to comprise part of a sleep switch (Morairty et al., 2004; Saper et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on mammalian sleep switches.

claim: The dorsal fan-shaped body (dFB) in Drosophila melanogaster has been suggested to play a role analogous to that of the mammalian VLPO.
source: Interestingly, even the smallest brains appear to have a sleep switch: in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, the dorsal fan-shaped body (dFB) has been suggested to play a role that is analogous to that of the mammalian VLPO (Donlea et al., 2014, 2018; Pimentel et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on the dFB.

claim: Activation of dFB neurons in the fly's central brain promotes sleep and achieves key sleep functions.
source: Indeed, activation of these neurons in the fly's central brain promotes sleep and achieves key sleep functions (Dissel et al., 2015; Donlea et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Changes in electrical activity in the fly brain are associated with spontaneous sleep transitions.
source: Recently, we have shown that changes in electrical activity in the fly brain are associated with spontaneous sleep transitions, and that activation of dFB neurons causes specific oscillatory signatures in local field potential (LFP) activity recorded from the central brain (Yap et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: Activation of dFB neurons causes specific oscillatory signatures in local field potential (LFP) activity recorded from the central brain.
source: Recently, we have shown that changes in electrical activity in the fly brain are associated with spontaneous sleep transitions, and that activation of dFB neurons causes specific oscillatory signatures in local field potential (LFP) activity recorded from the central brain (Yap et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: Decreased behavioral responsiveness appears to be a prerequisite for sleep induction.
source: Decreased behavioral responsiveness would appear to be a prerequisite for sleep induction
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between responsiveness and sleep.

claim: It remains unclear whether the same neurons could be involved in both acute loss of responsiveness and promotion of sleep functions.
source: but it remains unclear whether the same neurons could be involved in both acute loss of responsiveness and promotion of sleep functions (Lebestky et al., 2009)
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: Sleep is associated with decreased behavioral responsiveness.
source: While it is understood that sleep is associated with decreased behavioral responsiveness
evidence: This reflects established scientific understanding about sleep.

claim: It is unclear whether the Drosophila dFB plays a larger role in regulating arousal more generally, even in awake animals.
source: it is unclear whether the Drosophila dFB plays a larger role in regulating arousal more generally, even in awake animals.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Recent research identified a neurochemical mechanism for promoting sleep in Drosophila.
source: Recent research identified a neurochemical mechanism for promoting sleep in Drosophila (Donlea et al., 2018)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: It is unknown whether other pathways are employed to link internal sleep pressure signals in the dFB with the acute need to suppress behavioral responsiveness when flies need to sleep.
source: but it is unknown whether other pathways are employed to link effectively internal sleep pressure signals in the dFB with the acute need to suppress behavioral responsiveness when flies need to sleep.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Mammalian sleep processes might involve electrical signaling that is mediated via gap junctions.
source: In addition to neurochemical signaling from sleep centers such as the VLPO, mammalian sleep processes might also involve electrical signaling that is mediated via gap junctions (Coulon and Landisman, 2017; Franco-Pérez and Paz, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Gap-junction-mediated communication appears to be important for the rapid recruitment of much of the mammalian brain into synchronously firing networks.
source: Gap-junction-mediated communication appears to be important for the rapid recruitment of much of the mammalian brain into synchronously firing networks (Bennett and Zukin, 2004; Buzsaki, 2006)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: It remains unknown whether gap-junction-mediated communication is an important aspect of sleep physiology and function.
source: but it remains unknown whether this is an important aspect of sleep physiology and function.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: In vertebrates, connexin genes code for a variety of gap junction subtypes.
source: In vertebrates, connexin genes code for a variety of gap junction subtypes (Söhl and Willecke, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Invertebrates such as flies express a family of gap-junction genes that encode proteins called innexins.
source: Invertebrates such as flies express a family of gap-junction genes that encode proteins called innexins
evidence: This reflects established scientific knowledge about invertebrate gap junctions.

claim: Drosophila has eight innexin-encoding loci that have been implicated extensively in the development of the brain and other tissues.
source: and Drosophila has eight innexin-encoding loci that have been implicated extensively in the development of the brain and other tissues (Bauer et al., 2005; Stebbings et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In the adult fly, there is limited understanding of the role of gap-junction signaling in behavior.
source: In the adult fly, there is limited understanding of the role of gap-junction signaling in behavior
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge.

claim: Gap-junction signaling has a role in visual processing in Drosophila.
source: but studies have found a role for this signaling in visual processing (Cuntz et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2016a)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Gap-junction signaling has a role in escape behavior in Drosophila.
source: in escape behavior (Phelan et al., 1996)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Gap-junction signaling has a role in learning and memory in Drosophila.
source: and in learning and memory (Wu et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Sleep duration is measured by well-established inactivity criteria based on >5 min inactivity.
source: Sleep duration is measured by well-established inactivity criteria based on >5 min inactivity (Figure 1B, upper panel; Figure 1C) (Shaw et al., 2000)
evidence: This statement describes a standard method for measuring sleep in flies, supported by a citation and reference to figures.

claim: Behavioral responsiveness can be measured by tracking how flies respond to a mechanical stimulus, during both sleep or while they are awake.
source: whereas behavioral responsiveness can be measured by tracking how flies respond to a mechanical stimulus, during both sleep or while they are awake (van Alphen et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement describes a method for measuring behavioral responsiveness, supported by a citation.

claim: Following a vibration stimulus, responding flies typically increase their locomotion.
source: Following a vibration stimulus, responding flies typically increase their locomotion (Figure 1B, lower panel).
evidence: This statement describes an observed behavior, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: Average responses to mechanical stimuli are typically stronger during the day than during the night.
source: and average responses (mean peak responsiveness, see 'Materials and methods') are typically stronger during the day than during the night (Figure 1E, left and middle panel).
evidence: This statement describes an observed pattern in the data, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: Animals are by definition less responsive when they are asleep.
source: animals are by definition less responsive when they are asleep (Campbell and Tobler, 1984).
evidence: This statement reflects a definitional aspect of sleep, supported by a citation.

claim: Sleep duration and behavioral responsiveness were only negatively correlated at night, but not during the day in wildtype flies.
source: We found a surprisingly large amount of individual variability for these responsiveness and sleep metrics (Figure 1F). Sleep duration and behavioral responsiveness were only negatively correlated at night, but not during the day in the wildtype flies (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: The lack of daytime correlation between sleep duration and behavioral responsiveness could reflect a qualitative difference between daytime sleep and nighttime sleep.
source: While this could reflect a qualitative difference between daytime sleep and nighttime sleep (Faville et al., 2015)
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data, supported by a citation.

claim: The lack of daytime correlation between sleep duration and behavioral responsiveness might indicate that sleep bouts are generally longer at night.
source: or might indicate that sleep bouts are generally longer at night (Shaw et al., 2000)
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data, supported by a citation.

claim: Sleep duration and responsiveness might be separately controlled.
source: this also suggests that sleep duration and responsiveness might be separately controlled, as has been proposed by the authors of a previous study (Lebestky et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference from the data, supported by a citation.

claim: dFB activation is associated with increased arousal thresholds.
source: dFB activation is associated with increased arousal thresholds (Donlea et al., 2011, 2014; Pimentel et al., 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: It is unclear whether increased arousal thresholds are a direct feature of increased dFB activity or a consequence of other processes that result from increased dFB activity.
source: but it is unclear whether this is a direct feature of increased dFB activity or a consequence of other processes that result from increased dFB activity.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Chronic activation of the R23E10 neurons produced a strong negative correlation between sleep duration and behavioral responsiveness, even for daytime sleep.
source: Chronic activation of the R23E10 neurons produced a strong negative correlation between sleep duration and behavioral responsiveness, even for daytime sleep (Figure 1H): flies that slept more tended to respond less to stimuli, day or night.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: Genetic controls showed only a night-time correlation between sleep duration and behavioral responsiveness.
source: Genetic controls showed only a night-time correlation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), as seen in the wildtype background strain (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from control experiments, supported by reference to figures.

claim: C5 displayed a daytime correlation but not the nighttime correlation between sleep duration and behavioral responsiveness.
source: In contrast to data from R23E10, results with C5 and 104y were less clear: C5 displayed a daytime correlation but not the nighttime correlation
evidence: This is a finding from experiments with different Gal4 drivers, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: 104y did not display a daytime correlation between sleep duration and behavioral responsiveness.
source: and 104y did not display a daytime correlation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is a finding from experiments with different Gal4 drivers, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: R23E10 is a cleaner dFB driver than C5 and 104y.
source: This suggests that R23E10, which is a cleaner dFB driver (Jenett et al., 2012), may be more effective as a sleep switch.
evidence: This is an inference from the data, supported by a citation.

claim: The dFB might regulate behavioral responsiveness as well as sleep duration.
source: The R23E10 result also suggests that the dFB might regulate behavioral responsiveness as well as sleep duration
evidence: This is an inference from the R23E10 experimental results.

claim: Falling asleep is an acute event that happens within seconds in most animals.
source: Falling asleep is an acute event that happens within seconds in most animals (Campbell and Tobler, 1984)
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific understanding, supported by a citation.

claim: Flies can be significantly less responsive after only one minute of spontaneous quiescence.
source: and even flies can be significantly less responsive after only one minute of spontaneous quiescence (van Alphen et al., 2013; Faville et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Flies that were fed ATR significantly increased their sleep duration in response to dFB activation with prolonged red light exposure.
source: Flies that were fed ATR significantly increased their sleep duration in response to dFB activation with prolonged red light exposure (Figure 2A,B, blue).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's optogenetic experiments, supported by reference to figures.

claim: Behavioral responsiveness was robust in flies at baseline.
source: Behavioral responsiveness was robust in these flies at baseline (Figure 2C, left panel)
evidence: This is an observation from the study's experiments, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: Optogenetic activation of the dFB significantly decreased responsiveness to the vibration stimulus.
source: but optogenetic activation of the dFB significantly decreased responsiveness to the vibration stimulus (Figure 2C, right panel; Figure 2D, left panel).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's optogenetic experiments, supported by reference to figures.

claim: Responsiveness appeared to recover somewhat after several hours of red-light exposure.
source: Responsiveness was not, however, abolished by activation of the dFB, and even appeared to recover somewhat after several hours of red-light exposure (Figure 2C, right panel).
evidence: This is an observation from the study's experiments, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: Optogenetic activation of the 'sleep switch' increases sleep intensity.
source: Yet, as might be expected, optogenetic activation of the 'sleep switch' increases sleep intensity (Figure 2D, right panel; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) as well as sleep duration.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's optogenetic experiments, supported by reference to figures.

claim: dFB activation decreases behavioral responsiveness in awake flies as well as in sleeping flies.
source: We were surprised to find that dFB activation decreases behavioral responsiveness in awake flies as well as in sleeping flies (Figure 2E, right panel).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: Decreased responsiveness was not due to sluggish locomotion in awake animals.
source: Decreased responsiveness was not due to sluggish locomotion in awake animals: the walking speed of awake dFB-activated flies was not different from that of controls immediately preceding the vibration stimulus (Figure 2E, left panel, green shading).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments that rules out an alternative explanation, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: Behavioral responsiveness was significantly reduced after 1 min of red light.
source: In doing so, we found that behavioral responsiveness was significantly reduced after 1 min of red light, and that responsiveness was rapidly restored after the red light was turned off (Figure 2F)
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's acute optogenetic experiments, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: There was no evidence of sleep inertia following 5 min of dFB activation.
source: that is we observed no evidence of sleep inertia following 5 min of dFB activation.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments.

claim: Activation of the sleep switch suppresses behavioral responsiveness.
source: This shows that different stimulation regimes produce a similar effect and confirms that activation of the sleep switch suppresses behavioral responsiveness.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental conditions.

claim: The spiking activity of dFB soma responded to positive current steps by increasing their firing rate.
source: As shown previously (Donlea et al., 2014; Pimentel et al., 2016), the spiking activity of dFB soma responded to positive current steps by increasing their firing rate (Figure 3B, bottom left).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's electrophysiology experiments, supported by citations and reference to a figure.

claim: Not all dFB neurons shared the same spontaneous firing properties, with ~20% of the recorded cells identified as non-spiking.
source: However, not all neurons shared the same spontaneous firing properties, with ~20% of the recorded cells identified as non-spiking (even following current injection), whereas the remaining cells that did spike were observed to exhibit various combinations of single spikes and burst spiking patterns (Figure 3B, bottom right).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's electrophysiology experiments, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: CsChrimson-expressing cells all responded to a red-light stimulus in the same manner, by rapidly increasing their membrane potential upon activation.
source: Despite the heterogeneity in the firing pattern of the dFB neurons, CsChrimson-expressing cells all responded to a red-light stimulus in the same manner, by rapidly increasing their membrane potential upon activation, followed by a gradual return to its resting membrane state after the light was turned off (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's electrophysiology experiments, supported by reference to figures.

claim: 1 Hz pulsed activation increased the membrane potential in all CsChrimson-expressing dFB cells.
source: On average, 1 Hz pulsed activation also increased the membrane potential in all CsChrimson-expressing dFB cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's electrophysiology experiments, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: The acute dFB activation effects on behavioral responsiveness could be associated with increased membrane potential rather than with any specific increased spiking activity.
source: The robustness of this effect, despite the heterogeneity in the spontaneous firing pattern across cells and the different stimulus regimes, suggests that the acute dFB activation effects on behavioral responsiveness could be associated with increased membrane potential rather than with any specific increased spiking activity
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the electrophysiology data.

claim: The post-stimulation membrane potential was not significantly different from baseline.
source: Notably, the post-stimulation membrane potential (recorded only 1 min after the red light was turned off) was not significantly different from baseline (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is a finding from the study's electrophysiology experiments, supported by reference to figures.

claim: The acute effect on the membrane potential was not sustained for long after the stimulation.
source: indicating that the acute effect on the membrane potential was not sustained for long after the stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference from the electrophysiology data.

claim: Red light had no effect on spiking or the membrane potential in R23E10-Gal4/+ animals that had been fed ATR but that lacked channelrhodopsin.
source: Red light had no effect on spiking or the membrane potential in R23E10-Gal4/+ animals that had been fed ATR but that lacked channelrhodopsin (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, gray boxplots)
evidence: This is a finding from control experiments, supported by reference to figures.

claim: 1 Hz light pulses reliably evoked secondary and even tertiary spikes between 100 and 500 ms after the first evoked spike in a subset of recordings.
source: In a subset of recordings, 1 Hz light pulses reliably evoked secondary and even tertiary spikes between 100 and 500 ms after the first evoked spike (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), suggesting a reverberation in the circuit.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's electrophysiology experiments, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: An increased input resistance and membrane time constant in dFB cells has been shown to be associated with increased sleep pressure.
source: An increased input resistance and membrane time constant in dFB cells has been shown to be associated with increased sleep pressure (Donlea et al., 2014)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The optogenetic results are consistent with the idea that dFB cells form part of a sleep homeostat that is regulated by changing membrane potential levels.
source: so our optogenetic results are consistent with the idea that these cells form part of a sleep homeostat that is regulated by changing membrane potential levels (Pimentel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference from the study's results, supported by a citation.

claim: Output from the dFB cells regulates sleep duration by inhibiting a number of other systems in the central brain.
source: Recent work shows that output from the dFB cells regulates sleep duration by inhibiting a number of other systems in the central brain (Donlea et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2016b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: These communication channels from dFB are probably chemical in nature.
source: These communication channels are probably chemical in nature
evidence: This is an inference based on prior research.

claim: Transiently increasing synaptic activity in dFB neurons had no significant effect on behavioral responsiveness, or on sleep.
source: Interestingly, transiently increasing synaptic activity in dFB neurons (measured using temperature-sensitive syntaxin3-69 [Lagow et al., 2007; Kottler et al., 2013]) had no significant effect on behavioral responsiveness, or on sleep (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments with synaptic manipulations, supported by citations and reference to a figure.

claim: Transiently decreasing synaptic activity in the dFB decreased responsiveness, but equally so in the genetic controls.
source: Transiently decreasing synaptic activity (by using the temperature-sensitive shibire [Kitamoto, 2001]) in the dFB decreased responsiveness, but equally so in the genetic controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments with synaptic manipulations, supported by a citation and reference to a figure.

claim: A lack of clear effects using opposing synaptic manipulations suggests that (fast) chemical neurotransmission might not be a relevant mechanism employed by dFB neurons to control behavior acutely.
source: A lack of clear effects using these opposing synaptic manipulations suggests that (fast) chemical neurotransmission might not be a relevant mechanism employed by these neurons to control behavior acutely, or at least that these acute synaptic manipulations do not affect our behavioral readouts.
evidence: This is an inference from the synaptic manipulation experiments.

claim: A previous study has found expression of the gap junction gene, inx6, in the fan-shaped body.
source: A previous study has found expression of the gap junction gene, inx6, in the fan-shaped body (Wu et al., 2011)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: INX6 expression was seen most strongly in a dorsal layer of the fan-shaped body and in large cells in the pars intercerebralis (PI).
source: Expression was seen most strongly in a dorsal layer of the fan-shaped body and in large cells in the pars intercerebralis (PI) (Figure 4A, top and middle panels, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's immunochemistry experiments, supported by reference to figures.

claim: Co-labeling with GFP driven by R23E10-Gal4 revealed a significant overlap in the relevant dFB neurons (47.5% co-localization).
source: Co-labeling with GFP driven by R23E10-Gal4 revealed a significant overlap in the relevant dFB neurons (Figure 4B, bottom panel; a co-localization of 47.5% was found, see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a finding from the study's immunochemistry experiments, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: No evidence of co-localization of INX6 was found in the dFB cell soma.
source: However, we did not find any evidence of co-localization in the dFB cell soma (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's immunochemistry experiments, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: Dye-fill experiments confirmed that the dFB neurons are coupled to other cells via gap junctions.
source: Dye-fill experiments confirmed that the dFB neurons are coupled to other cells via gap junctions (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C; Video 1)
evidence: This is a finding from the study's dye-coupling experiments, supported by reference to a figure and video.

claim: Only the large PI cells above the dFB revealed any reliable dye coupling in the experiments.
source: although the extent of this electrically coupled network remains unclear as only the large PI cells above the dFB revealed any reliable dye coupling in our experiments.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's dye-coupling experiments.

claim: Flies expressing the INX6 RNAi construct in the dFB showed a decrease in both day and night sleep.
source: Flies expressing the INX6 RNAi construct in the dFB showed a decrease in both day and night sleep (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's INX6 knockdown experiments, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: Flies slept less deeply and were more responsive to stimuli when INX6 was downregulated in the dFB.
source: Flies slept less deeply and were more responsive to stimuli when INX6 was downregulated in the dFB (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's INX6 knockdown experiments, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: INX6-knockdown flies could still achieve deeper sleep stages after 16–20 min immobility.
source: Closer examination of sleep intensity as a function of time asleep (van Alphen et al., 2013) showed that INX6-knockdown flies could still achieve deeper sleep stages (e.g. after 16–20 min immobility, Figure 5C), although these flies slept more lightly in general.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's INX6 knockdown experiments, supported by a citation and reference to a figure.

claim: INX6 plays a role in suppressing behavioral responsiveness during lighter sleep stages.
source: This suggests that INX6 plays a role in suppressing behavioral responsiveness during lighter sleep stages, whereas during deeper sleep, the role of INX6 might be less important.
evidence: This is an inference from the sleep intensity data.

claim: Knocking down INX6 in adult flies significantly increased daytime behavioral responsiveness and decreased daytime sleep intensity, but had no significant effect on sleep duration.
source: Knocking down INX6 in the adult dFB significantly increased daytime behavioral responsiveness and decreased daytime sleep intensity, but had no significant effect on sleep duration (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's adult-specific INX6 knockdown experiments, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: INX6 is important for communicating dFB activity levels to regulate behavioral responsiveness.
source: These results suggest that INX6 is important for communicating dFB activity levels to regulate behavioral responsiveness.
evidence: This is an inference from the INX6 knockdown experiments.

claim: Reduced INX6 expression in the dFB did not impair CsChrimson-mediated cell activation.
source: Whole-cell recordings revealed that reduced INX6 expression in the dFB (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) did not impair CsChrimson-mediated cell activation: a significant increase in membrane potential was still observed with constant red light as well as with 1 Hz pulses (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's electrophysiology experiments with INX6 knockdown, supported by reference to figures.

claim: The increase of the membrane potential in activated dFB neurons does not depend upon INX6 expression in these cells.
source: This shows that the increase of the membrane potential in activated dFB neurons does not depend upon INX6 expression in these cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the electrophysiology data with INX6 knockdown.

claim: 40% of wildtype dFB cells exhibited reliable secondary spikes 100–500 ms after a light-evoked action potential.
source: Nevertheless, we did observe some intracellular differences: whereas 40% of wildtype dFB cells exhibited reliable secondary spikes 100–500 ms after a light-evoked action potential (Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is a finding from the study's electrophysiology experiments, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: None of the INX6 knocked-down cells displayed secondary spikes within 100-500 ms after a light-evoked action potential.
source: none of the INX6 knocked-down cells displayed secondary spikes within that timeframe (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's electrophysiology experiments with INX6 knockdown, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: There was considerably less variability in the membrane potential for dFB cells lacking INX6.
source: Also, we noted considerably less variability in the membrane potential for dFB cells lacking INX6 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6C,D right panels, compared with Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's electrophysiology experiments with INX6 knockdown, supported by reference to figures.

claim: Optogenetic dFB activation using R23E10-Gal4 produces increased LFP activity in the fly brain, especially in low (1–15 Hz) frequencies.
source: We have shown previously that optogenetic dFB activation using the same R23E10-Gal4 driver produces increased LFP activity in the fly brain, especially in low (1–15 Hz) frequencies, and that oscillations within this range are also seen during transitions to spontaneous sleep in flies (Yap et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: In flies with INX6 knocked down in the dFB, there was no increased LFP activity upon optogenetic activation.
source: In flies with INX6 knocked down in the dFB, however, there was no increased LFP activity (Figure 6E, bottom panel; Figure 6F, purple)
evidence: This is a finding from the study's LFP experiments with INX6 knockdown, supported by reference to figures.

claim: 1 Hz stimulation of R23E10-Gal4 neurons produced an LFP signature in the dFB, evident as an event-related potential (ERP).
source: 1 Hz stimulation of R23E10-Gal4 neurons also produced an LFP signature in the dFB, evident as an event-related potential (ERP) (Figure 6G, blue).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's LFP experiments, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: INX6 knockdown in R23E10 neurons significantly blunted the amplitude of the 1 Hz ERP.
source: Consistent with our results using a constant red-light activation regime, INX6 knockdown in R23E10 neurons significantly blunted the amplitude of the 1 Hz ERP (Figure 6G, purple).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's LFP experiments with INX6 knockdown, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: One important consequence of INX6 knockdown in the sleep-promoting R23E10 cells is decreased synchronous activity in the dFB.
source: Together, these results suggest that one important consequence of INX6 knockdown in the sleep-promoting R23E10 cells is decreased synchronous activity in the dFB (detected as LFPs), whereas the activation effects on the membrane potential measured at the soma remain robust.
evidence: This is an inference from the LFP and whole-cell recording data.

claim: Perfusion of CBX onto the brain blunted the ERP recorded from the dFB.
source: Perfusion of CBX onto the brain blunted the ERP recorded from the dFB, as did locally injected CBX (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's gap junction blocker experiments, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: Gap junctions are required to produce synchronized activity in the dFB.
source: This adds further evidence that gap junctions are required to produce synchronized activity in the dFB.
evidence: This is an inference from the CBX experiments.

claim: Optogenetically activating the dFB in cells where INX6 was knocked down still caused an increase in sleep duration and bout length compared to negative control flies.
source: Optogenetically activating the dFB in cells where INX6 was knocked down still caused an increase in sleep duration and bout length compared to those in negative control flies (Figure 7A,B, purple compared to black).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's combined optogenetic and INX6 knockdown experiments, supported by reference to figures.

claim: The sleep-promoting effect of dFB activation with INX6 knockdown was not as strong as the activation of the dFB circuit with functional INX6.
source: This effect was, however, not as strong as the activation of the dFB circuit with functional INX6 in these cells (Figure 7A,B, blue).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's combined optogenetic and INX6 knockdown experiments, supported by reference to figures.

claim: INX6 knockdown blunts the sleep-promoting effect of dFB activation.
source: This shows that INX6 knockdown blunts the sleep-promoting effect of dFB activation.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined optogenetic and INX6 knockdown experiments.

claim: Behavioral responsiveness was significantly decreased when the dFB was activated whereas INX6 expression was intact.
source: Correspondingly, behavioral responsiveness was significantly decreased when the dFB was activated whereas INX6 expression was intact (Figure 7C,D blue).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's combined optogenetic and INX6 knockdown experiments, supported by reference to figures.

claim: INX6 knockdown completely blocked the effect of dFB activation on behavioral responsiveness.
source: However, clear differences were evident upon red-light activation: in contrast to the partial effects on sleep duration, INX6 knockdown completely blocked the effect of dFB activation on behavioral responsiveness (Figure 7C, purple) measured in terms of either mean peak responsiveness and sleep intensity (Figure 7D, purple)
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's combined optogenetic and INX6 knockdown experiments, supported by reference to figures.

claim: INX6 expression is required for the sleep switch to downregulate behavioral responsiveness acutely, but INX6 is not required for these neurons to be sleep promoting.
source: These activation experiments therefore uncover a dissociation between behavioral responsiveness and sleep duration: INX6 expression is required for the sleep switch to downregulate behavioral responsiveness acutely, but INX6 is not required for these neurons to be sleep promoting.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion drawn from the combined optogenetic and INX6 knockdown experiments.

claim: dFB neurons are still able to affect sleep duration via other mechanisms when INX6 is knocked down.
source: Presumably, dFB neurons are still able to affect sleep duration via other mechanisms (Donlea et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results, supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mechanisms that regulate behavioral responsiveness are likely to be involved during transitions from wakefulness to sleep.
source: Mechanisms that regulate behavioral responsiveness are therefore likely to be involved during transitions from wakefulness to sleep
evidence: This is a logical inference about sleep mechanisms.

claim: It seems parsimonious that overlapping neuronal systems might govern both behavioral responsiveness and sleep.
source: so it seems parsimonious that overlapping neuronal systems might govern both behavioral states.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the organization of sleep systems.

claim: Sleep onset has some similarity with selective attention in its capacity to gate or suppress perception rapidly.
source: In this way, sleep onset has some similarity with selective attention in its capacity to gate or suppress perception rapidly (Kirszenblat and van Swinderen, 2015).
evidence: This is a conceptual comparison supported by a citation.

claim: Gap junctions expressed in the sleep-promoting neurons of the dFB are probably mediators for gating behavioral responsiveness in both awake and sleeping flies.
source: We show here that gap junctions that are expressed in the sleep-promoting neurons of the dFB in the central fly brain are probably mediators for gating behavioral responsiveness in both awake and sleeping flies, as a consequence of acutely increased membrane potential in these neurons.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study's experiments.

claim: Increased sleep pressure increases the input resistance and membrane time constants in dFB neurons.
source: Recent work has shown that sleep pressure increases the input resistance and membrane time constants in these same neurons (Donlea et al., 2014; Pimentel et al., 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Increased sleep pressure impairs behavioral responsiveness via electrical channels, perhaps even before promoting and maintaining sleep.
source: so this seems to be a probable mechanism whereby increased sleep pressure impairs behavioral responsiveness via electrical channels, perhaps even before promoting and maintaining sleep — which may then occur via chemical (e.g. peptidergic) signaling from these neurons (Donlea et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study's findings, supported by a citation.

claim: The R23E10 neurons have two distinct arousal-related functions: to regulate behavioral responsiveness more generally and to maintain sleep for the duration required by homeostatic demands.
source: It is therefore possible that the R23E10 neurons, which have been recently characterized as comprising part of a 'sleep homeostat' in the fly brain (Donlea et al., 2018; Pimentel et al., 2016), have two distinct arousal-related functions: to regulate behavioral responsiveness more generally — and thus to promote sleep acutely — and then to maintain sleep for the duration required by homeostatic demands.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study's findings, supported by citations.

claim: dFB-mediated suppression of behavioral responsiveness could be a prequel to sleep.
source: However, our data suggest that dFB-mediated suppression of behavioral responsiveness could be a prequel to sleep.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Sleep intensity was increased upon prolonged dFB activation, suggesting a distinct cumulative effect.
source: Sleep intensity was increased however upon prolonged dFB activation, suggesting a distinct cumulative effect.
evidence: This is an inference from the study's prolonged activation experiments.

claim: At the deepest stage of sleep, removal of INX6 from the dFB had no effect on behavioral responsiveness.
source: Indeed, at the deepest stage of sleep (when flies are least responsive to mechanical stimuli), removal of INX6 from the dFB had no effect on behavioral responsiveness (Figure 5C), suggesting that other factors are involved at that stage for maintaining high arousal thresholds.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's INX6 knockdown experiments, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: When flies are closer to awakening or engaged in lighter sleep stages, INX6-mediated mechanisms come back into play to maintain sleep.
source: When flies are closer to awakening again, or when they are engaged in lighter sleep stages, it is possible that INX6-mediated mechanisms come back into play to maintain sleep.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the sleep intensity data.

claim: Transitions in and out of sleep are associated with dFB activity.
source: In recent work, we have shown that transitions in and out of sleep are associated with dFB activity (Yap et al., 2017)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: Other dFB neurons outside of the R23E10 circuit are also likely involved in regulating behavioral responsiveness.
source: It is likely that other dFB neurons outside of the R23E10 circuit are also involved, as suggested by only partial overlap with INX6 labeling (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an inference from the immunochemistry data, supported by reference to a figure.

claim: Without INX6, activated R23E10 neurons were unable to reduce behavioral responsiveness, suggesting a cell-autonomous effect.
source: However, without INX6, activated R23E10 neurons were unable to reduce behavioral responsiveness, suggesting a cell-autonomous effect.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined optogenetic and INX6 knockdown experiments.

claim: dFB activation is associated with increased LFP activity in the central brain, which could reflect increased synchronous neural firing.
source: We have shown here and elsewhere (Yap et al., 2017) that dFB activation is associated with increased LFP activity in the central brain, which could reflect increased synchronous neural firing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the LFP data, supported by a citation.

claim: Without expression of INX6 in the R23E10 neurons, induced LFP effects disappear, suggesting that gap junctions are important for promoting synchronous activity in this circuit.
source: Without expression of INX6 in the R23E10 neurons, these induced LFP effects also disappear, suggesting that gap junctions are important for promoting synchronous activity in this circuit.
evidence: This is an inference from the LFP data with INX6 knockdown.

claim: The dFB might suppress behavioral responsiveness upon sleep onset by producing synchronous low frequency activity that could interfere with ongoing sensory processing and integration in the central brain.
source: This suggests a rapid mechanism through which the dFB might suppress behavioral responsiveness upon sleep onset, by for example producing synchronous low frequency activity that could interfere with ongoing sensory processing and integration in the central brain.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the LFP findings.

claim: Electrical communication to other cells via gap junctions could support subtler levels of behavioral control while the flies are awake.
source: Although acute activation of the R23E10 neurons alone is unlikely to occur in a natural context, electrical communication to other cells via gap junctions could support subtler levels of behavioral control while the flies are awake, which might consolidate into overall increased arousal thresholds as membrane potentials across the dFB increase with increasing sleep pressure.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Cells in the pars intercerebralis (PI) are probably involved in the gap-junction-coupled network with dFB neurons.
source: Future studies should uncover the extent of this gap-junction-coupled network, although our antibody-labeling (Figure 4) and dye-coupling experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) suggest that cells in the pars intercerebralis (PI) are probably involved.
evidence: This is an inference from the immunochemistry and dye-coupling data, supported by reference to figures.

claim: It remains possible that dFB neurons are electrically coupled to each other, thereby generating LFP oscillations that are employed in the regulation of behavior.
source: It also remains possible that dFB neurons are electrically coupled to each other, thereby generating LFP oscillations that are employed in the regulation of behavior.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism of LFP generation.

claim: In dye-coupling experiments, no evidence of labeling of another dFB cell was seen, whereas multiple PI cells were labeled.
source: However, in our dye-coupling experiments (see 'Materials and methods'), we did not see any evidence of labeling of another dFB cell, whereas multiple PI cells were labeled.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's dye-coupling experiments.

claim: It is not known whether electrical communication might be employed to promote sleep in other animal brains.
source: It is not known whether electrical communication might be employed to promote sleep in other animal brains
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge.

claim: There is increasing evidence that gap junctions play an important role in the regulation of behavioral state and arousal in the mammalian brain.
source: although there is increasing evidence that gap junctions play an important role in the regulation of behavioral state and arousal in the mammalian brain (Coulon and Landisman, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A role for gap junctions in sleep-promoting neurons suggests a novel plasticity mechanism for regulating behavioral states.
source: More generally, a role for gap junctions in sleep-promoting neurons also suggests a novel plasticity mechanism for regulating behavioral states.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: The parallel electrical communication channel afforded by gap junctions could provide an alternate way of regulating sleep pressure.
source: Whereas plasticity is typically viewed as a property of chemical synapses, the parallel electrical communication channel afforded by gap junctions could provide an alternate way of regulating sleep pressure, and thereby promoting sleep functions while ensuring that arousal thresholds are tightly linked to sleep need.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Transient electrical activation of the dFB neurons during fly brain development permanently impairs behavioral responsiveness in adult animals.
source: In recent work, we have shown that transient electrical activation of the dFB neurons during fly brain development permanently impairs behavioral responsiveness in adult animals (Ferguson et al., 2017)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: Different INX6 expression levels in the dFB may provide a mechanism for optimally linking behavioral responsiveness with sleep need.
source: Different INX6 expression levels in the dFB may provide a mechanism for optimally linking behavioral responsiveness with sleep need.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the role of INX6 expression levels.
